text.p: Winterthur Insurance Co on Wednesday said 1996 group net profit jumped 21 percent to 506.7 million Swiss francs ($351 million), rounding off strong performances last year by big Swiss insurers.
Winterthur proposed a dividend of 21 Swiss francs per share, up 10.5 percent from 19 Swiss francs.
The company's 1996 earnings per share of 57 Swiss francs result was at the upper end of forecasts between 54 and 60 Swiss francs by financial analysts.

But the growth was below some expectations on the stock market, which had been boosted by net profit leaps of 30 percent at Zurich Insurance on April 30 and 33 percent at reinsurance giant Swiss Re on May 2.
"After rising some 15 percent in the past three weeks, there could be some short-term Winterthur selling now," Bank Baer analyst Beat Alpiger told Reuters.
Winterthur registered shares closed at 1,128 Swiss francs, down by three, just before the results were announced.

But Alpiger said it was clear the big Swiss insurers, who have busily reorganised over the past two or three years to cut costs and focus on promising businesses, were placed among the global winners of deregulation and consolidation in the industry.
"It looks as though the big insurers have cleared up the problems they had in the past," Alpiger said.

Winterthur's steps last year included bringing Swiss operations under one common management and reinforcing European markets as well as winning the first licence for a European insurer to operate in China.
Winterthur said its 1996 results included a 16 percent rise in gross premiums to 25.9 billion Swiss francs, including more than 15 billion in non-life business and over 10 billion in life premiums.
Financial results were up 18 percent to 5.5 billion Swiss francs thanks in large part to an increase in stock investments and "a greater international diversification in assets in the past few years.
"The current investment income (interest, dividends) registered a solid development with growth of 15 percent," it added in a statement.
"The company's policy of actively managing foreign currencies also led to considerable gains on exchange rate differences," Winterthur said.
Investments totalled 85.6 billion Swiss francs, up 19 percent, and technical provisions were 19 percent higher at 80.4 billion.
Shareholder equity grew more than one billion Swiss francs to 5.2 billion.
"The main contributory factors to this growth of 28 percent were foreign currency appreciation, the wider margins on stocks and the rise of annual profit," Winterthur said.
Winterthur said it would present more detailed numbers on 1996 results at an annual news conference and a separate presentation to financial analysts on May 29. ($ = 1.445 Swiss Francs)
